Hi Oliver — thanks, happy to run a demo. One quick ask: can you confirm which timezone you mean by '10:00'? That small ambiguity causes cross-region calendar mixups (Outlook/Google sometimes show different offsets). To avoid that, below are concrete options (all for Tue, 23 Mar):

Option A (morning CET): 10:00 CET / 09:00 UTC / 02:00 PDT / 05:00 EDT
Option B (midday CET): 12:00 CET / 11:00 UTC / 04:00 PDT / 07:00 EDT
Option C (afternoon CET): 15:00 CET / 14:00 UTC / 07:00 PDT / 10:00 EDT

If you're in Milan (CET) and meant local 10:00, Option A is the one we'll book. If your team prefers a US-friendly time for East Coast attendees, Option C maps to 10:00 ET.

Small note on DST: the US switched to DST on 8 Mar (we're on PDT/EDT), Europe switches later on 29 Mar (CEST). For Tue 23 Mar the Europe side is still CET (UTC+1), so the conversions above are correct for that date.

If you confirm which of A/B/C (or give an explicit timezone like "10:00 CET" or "10:00 UTC") I'll send a calendar invite with the timezone embedded and an agenda PDF.

Thanks —

Chloe — I'll be on the call. One small cautioned note we've seen with enterprise Outlook clients: when organizers set the invite to a named zone (e.g., Europe/Rome) some Outlook clients accidentally show the invite one hour earlier after the DST boundary if the recipient's machine tz settings are set to use auto DST updates. To avoid confusion for mixed-client teams I sometimes do two things:

1) Add the meeting in UTC in the calendar (i.e. event time set to 09:00 UTC) and put the local equivalents in the invite text (10:00 CET / 05:00 EDT etc).
2) Add a one-line note in the event description: "Event time = 09:00 UTC (10:00 Europe/Rome). If your calendar shows a different local time, verify your OS/timezone settings or view in the browser calendar."

If it's OK with you, Chloe, I'll send a quick duplicate invite set to UTC; that method has reduced cross-client confusion on previous calls.
